title: One Family Becomes Many Nations
overview: This chapter traces the peoples known to ancient Israel back to Noah's three sons, sketching a family map of the world after the flood.

parts.label: Japheth's peoples (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: These names mostly match peoples to Israel's north and west: Madai is the Medes, Javan the Greeks, and Kittim probably Cyprus. The 'coastlands' or 'maritime peoples' were lands reached by sea, around the Mediterranean and Asia Minor.

parts.label: Ham's peoples (vv. 6-7, 13-20)
parts.note: These lie mostly to the south: Cush is the upper Nile region, Mizraim is Egypt, and Put is probably Libya. Canaan's clans get the most detail because they were Israel's close neighbors in the land Israel would later live in, and the grouping seems to follow geography and political ties more than language.

parts.label: Nimrod the empire builder (vv. 8-12)
parts.note: Nimrod is remembered as a famous warrior who founded cities in Babylonia, including Babylon, Uruk and Akkad, then spread into Assyria and built Nineveh. 'Before the LORD' may simply mean 'in God's sight' or 'very great'; later tradition often painted him as a proud rebel, but the text itself does not clearly say that.

parts.label: Shem and Eber (vv. 21-25)
parts.note: Shem's line includes Elam, Ashur (Assyria) and Aram (the Arameans of Syria), and Eber is singled out because his name is usually linked with 'Hebrew,' pointing ahead to Abraham's family. Peleg's name sounds like the Hebrew word for 'divide'; scholars are unsure whether it refers to the scattering at Babel, a division of land, or something else.

parts.label: Joktan's Arabian tribes (vv. 26-31)
parts.note: Joktan's sons mostly match tribes of the Arabian peninsula, including Sheba, Ophir and Havilah, places later known for trade and gold. The exact locations of Mesha and Sephar are uncertain.

parts.label: All nations from one family (v. 32)
parts.note: Jewish tradition counts about seventy nations here, and many readers take that number as a way of picturing the whole world. The list presents every people as sharing one ancestry, and because chapter 11 goes on to tell how the scattering happened, many scholars think the two chapters are arranged by theme rather than in strict time order.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this list is a literal family record of individual descendants or a stylized map that organizes known peoples by region and relationship using the language of family.
think: This chapter places every people it knows inside one family tree; does thinking of strangers as distant relatives change anything for you, and why or why not?
